old: Women naturally carry 6-11% more body fat than men. This is biologically essential for hormone production, reproductive health, and breast tissue. A woman at BMI 22 typically has about 25% body fat, while a man at the same BMI may have only 18%.
new: At the same BMI, women typically carry a higher percentage of body fat than men, which supports hormone production and reproductive health. The relationship between BMI and body fat differs by sex (CDC NCHS).

old:
Low Testosterone at High BMI

Research shows a strong inverse relationship between BMI and testosterone levels in men. Excess body fat -- particularly visceral fat -- converts testosterone to estrogen through the aromatase enzyme. Men with a BMI over 30 are up to 2.4 times more likely to have low testosterone (hypogonadism) compared to men with a BMI under 25. Low testosterone can further promote fat storage and muscle loss, creating a negative feedback loop. This is discussed in detail by.

old: On June 17, 1998, approximately 29 million Americans who had gone to bed at a "healthy weight" woke up classified as "overweight" — without gaining a single pound. The change increased the percentage of American adults classified as overweight from about 40% to 55%.
new: In 1998, the NHLBI's clinical guidelines defined overweight as a BMI of 25 to 29.9, so millions of Americans who had been considered normal weight were reclassified as overweight without gaining a pound. Under the new definitions, about 55% of US adults were overweight or obese in NHANES III: 32.6% overweight and 22.3% with obesity (NHLBI Evidence Report, 1998).

old: The Boer formula is a population-based estimate and can vary by 5-10% from actual measurements. It is most accurate for people of average body composition and less accurate for very lean or very obese individuals. Compared to other estimation formulas (James, Hume), the Boer formula generally produces results closest to DEXA scan measurements across the widest range of body types. For precise measurements, clinical methods like DEXA scanning, hydrostatic weighing, or air displacement plethysmography are recommended. The formula is best used as a screening tool or for tracking general trends rather than as an absolute measurement.
new: The Boer formula is a population-based estimate: it predicts lean body mass from height and weight, so individual results can differ from measured values, especially for very lean, very muscular or very heavy people. For precise measurements, clinical methods like DEXA scanning, hydrostatic weighing, or air displacement plethysmography are recommended. The formula is best used as a screening tool or for tracking general trends rather than as an absolute measurement.
